name: Kivval
tagline: Car buying and ownership in Colombia, made transparent.
cardResult: 35k people in year one · ~US$200k GMV · break-even in 2024
coverAlt: Kivval web app home page with car search and ownership steps

star.situation: Buying a car in Colombia meant visiting dealers one by one and guessing what the car would really cost to own.
star.task: Build one place that shows the full cost before you buy, and stays useful after.
star.action: We launched a mobile MVP, saw the app itself was the barrier, moved to the web, and shifted from buying to ownership services.
star.result: 35k people in year one, ~US$200k in vehicles sold (GMV), break-even in 2024.

items.alt: Kivval app flow: search, compare, buy and Mi Kivval screens
items.caption: The mobile MVP flow: search, compare, buy, then manage the car in Mi Kivval.

sections.title: The insight
sections.body: After seeing the full comparison, people bought wherever the car was cheapest, so the purchase commission was small. The real pain, and the bigger market, was ownership: insurance, SOAT, taxes, oil, brakes and tires. So Kivval grew from comparing cars into managing them.

sections.title: Four decisions
items: **Mobile app to web app (2024).** Store data and research both showed people dropped off at the download.
**Cut the launch discount.** It drove first purchases, not loyalty, so we moved that budget to partner benefits.
**Built B2B partnerships** for financing, insurance, designated drivers and car washes.
**Cut Kivval+.** The US$5/month plan (washes, parking, designated drivers) didn't get the engagement it needed.

sections.title: What I learned
sections.body: I wanted Kivval to become an AI-driven tech company with stronger marketing; my co-founders wanted to stay closer to a dealership model. We saw different futures and parted ways in 2025. Effort can't make up for a vision the leaders don't share, so now I align vision, roadmap and roles before anything gets built.

name: Disney Parks
tagline: Keeping a core platform shipping, sprint after sprint.
cardResult: 10+ features per PI · releases every 2 weeks · team of 20, 7 connected teams

star.situation: Partners had to ask our team every time they wanted a new product online, and business requirements kept drifting away from the technical criteria dev and QA built against.
star.task: Remove both bottlenecks without slowing down a platform the business depends on.
star.action: I changed the partner UI so partners create their own products, and moved PRDs into an AI-assisted repo where requirements and technical criteria are checked against each other before each sprint.
star.result: 10+ features per PI · releases every 2 weeks · a team of 20 working with 7 connected teams

sections.title: How the work flows
items: Business requirements
PRD in the monorepo
Architecture design
AI gap analysis
Task breakdown: product, delivery, tech
AI-drafted Jira tickets
Refinement and estimation
Capacity plan and sprint goals
Build, QA, E2E and UAT
Release and production monitoring

sections.title: Four decisions
items: **Partners create their own products.** I changed the UI so partners add and create products themselves, instead of contacting our team every time.
**Requirements and technical criteria in one repo.** Discrepancies show up before the sprint starts, not during QA.
**AI drafts the tickets, people review them.** Speed from AI with project context; accuracy from refinement.
**Other teams' testing time is part of our plan.** Every platform connects to this one, so their integration windows are built into ours.

sections.title: What changed
sections.body: Business and technical acceptance criteria now match before work starts, so dev and QA get clear requirements and the code reflects what the business asked for.

sections.title: Earlier on Disney (Jul 2022–May 2024)
sections.body: Led product and delivery for 5 teams (~25 people) in online ticketing and US parks. Designed the opportunities-management process for Globant's Disney PMs, later adopted as a standard across LATAM.

name: SGF · Acero y Concreto
tagline: One cash view for a group of companies.
cardResult: Replacing a 15-year-old Excel · 3 of 4 sprints delivered · go-live Oct 15
coverAlt: SGF review screen: income and expenses grouped by cost center, with totals and a review mark per row

star.situation: A construction group ran the cash of several companies from one Excel built over 15 years. It took about 5 minutes to open, and duplicate or misfiled payments slipped through.
star.task: Replace it with a simple system that keeps each company's money apart and shows real balances by cost center.
star.action: We built our own tool instead of adapting single-company accounting software, made every entry start with the company so a payment can't land in the wrong project, and kept accounting out of scope.

numbers.label: age of the Excel it replaces
invoices a month still on paper

items.alt: New expense form: company first, then cost center and bank account filtered to it
items.caption: Company first: cost center and bank account only show what belongs to it.

items.alt: Reports matrix with income, expenses and margin by company and cost center
items.caption: Balances by company and cost center, not a flat list.

sections.title: The insight
sections.body: Most errors in the Excel weren't typos. They came from being able to pair any payment with any company, cost center or bank account. Once every form starts with the company and filters the rest, that kind of error can't happen, so the monthly review can focus on what's left: duplicates.

items.label: changes from the first demo, all built in the next sprint
watching the admin review a month, which became the review screen
with the treasurer: saving keeps her on a clean form for the next entry

items.after: pick the company, the system links the rest
the client adds banks in settings

sections.title: Four decisions
items: **Build, not buy.** Alegra, Siigo and Xero are made for one company's accounting. The group needed cash control across several companies, with its own categories.
**Not an accounting system.** One running number per record, no ledger rules. The client said it plainly: this platform isn't accounting.
**Paper to digital in two steps.** Accountants handle ~300 invoices a month on paper, so first the system prints the format they already use.
**Hide columns, don't cut them.** The admin wanted all the data, so each user hides what they don't need.

sections.title: What I learned
sections.body: The hard part wasn't the software. It was moving people off a tool they built themselves, so every step keeps something familiar until the new way earns trust.

name: Qiddiya City
tagline: B2B ticketing for Saudi Arabia's new theme parks.
cardResult: MVP launched for 3 parks · checkout, catalog and search · team of 32

star.situation: Qiddiya City's new parks needed travel agencies and partners to buy tickets online, one at a time or in bulk.
star.task: Take a B2B ticketing platform from discovery to MVP launch.
star.action: I mapped how partners buy, shaped the catalog, search by park and date, and checkout, and held the launch date by trading new scope for planned work.
star.result: MVP launched for 3 parks · team of 32

numbers.label: people across web, backend, QA, UX and DevOps

sections.title: What I shaped
items: **Checkout:** cart, card details, an order summary and payment.
**Catalog and search:** partners find tickets by park and by date.
**Partner accounts:** onboarding, saved payment methods and B2B credit lines for later purchases.
**Integrations:** CRM, CMS, the ticketing system and the payment gateway. I was on site through UAT to answer product questions.

sections.title: One decision
sections.body: The client wanted more features in the MVP. I made the rule explicit: new scope in means something comes out. We added the CMS integrations and richer image and video content for advertising, and gave up accessibility, performance and UI enhancements in the MVP to keep the launch date.

name: The Beer World
tagline: A craft-beer marketplace for a global brewer.
cardResult: Earned a job offer · €491k MVP plan
coverAlt: The Beer World prototype home page

star.situation: Craft breweries were taking share from Rook, a 150-year-old brewer, and most of them refused to be bought.
star.task: Find a way for Rook into craft beer without buying breweries or brewing new beers.
star.action: I designed a two-sided marketplace that gives brewers reach under their own name, scoped a lean 8-month MVP, and built a working prototype.
star.result: A strategy case that earned me a job offer · €491k MVP plan

sections.title: The insight
sections.body: Craft brewers don't want to sell, because a corporate owner kills their authenticity. So Rook shouldn't own them; it should give them reach. The platform tells each brewer's story under their own name, and Rook enters craft beer through commissions and data instead of acquisitions.

sections.title: Who it's for
items: **Beer lovers:** millennials who value origin and experience but lack time to find local breweries. The pain sits in exploring and in buying.
**Brewers:** dependent on social media, with no marketing budget, digital tools or data.
**Research plan:** surveys, interviews and focus groups in month 1, design validation in month 3, usability tests in months 6–8.

items.alt: Customer journey map hypothesis for beer lovers
items.caption: Journey map hypothesis for beer lovers.

sections.title: Four decisions
items: **Core experience before a full catalog.** Launch faster, accept some tech debt, let real users shape what's next.
**Pilot in the UK, Germany and France first,** the largest craft markets.
**Brewers handle logistics; no brewer CMS or CRM in the MVP.** Keeps the first release lean.
**Revenue beyond the 15% commission:** subscriptions, a brewer data dashboard, promoted placements.

sections.title: Risks I'd test first
sections.body: Alcohol rules per country, delivery logistics and user acquisition cost.

footer: Built solo: strategy, roadmap, cost model and prototype.

name: Lead CRM
tagline: Turning campaign leads into a reusable customer base.
cardResult: 5 pilot clients · one clear lesson on tradeoffs
coverAlt: Lead CRM dashboard with clients per month and per sector

star.situation: A marketing agency's clients lost their campaign leads once a campaign ended, with nowhere to reuse them for remarketing or email.
star.task: Build a simple CRM so those leads stay useful.
star.action: I built it in Bubble. When we found the agency had no CRM either, I added a first question at sign-up: agency or business?
star.result: Tested with 5 clients · stopped when the agency chose not to continue

items.alt: Sign-up screen asking whether you are a marketing agency or a business
items.caption: The pivot, in the product: agency or business?

items.alt: New client form in the Lead CRM
items.caption: Adding a lead.

sections.title: What I learned
sections.body: The agency wanted a robust platform in one month. When scope, time and budget don't match, someone has to say so on day one: cut scope, add people, or call it not feasible. Now I have that conversation before any build starts.
